source_text: Hunc si pater misit in similitudinem carnis peccati, non ideo phantasma dicetur caro, quae in illo uidebatur. peccatum enim carni supra adscripsit et illam fecit legem peccati habitantem in membris suis et aduersantem legi sensus. ob hoc igitur missum filium in similitudinem carnis peccati, ut peccati carnem simili substantia redimeret, id est carne, quae peccatrici carni similis esset, cum peccatrix ipsa non esset. nam et haec erit dei uirtus in substantia pari perficere salutem. non enim magnum, si spiritus dei carnem remediaret, sed si caro, consimilis peccatrici, dum caro est, sed non peccati. ita similitudo ad titulum peccati pertinebit, non ad substantiae mendacium. nam nec addidisset 'peccati', si substantiae similitudinem uellet intellegi, ut negaret ueritatem; tantum enim (carnis) posuisset, non et (peccat ? . cum uero tunc sic struxit: 'carnis peccati', et substantiam confirmauit, id est carnem, et similitudinem ad uitium substantiae retulit, id est ad peccatum. puta nunc similitudinem substantiae dictam: non ideo negabitur substantiae ueritas. (cur ergo similis, (si) uera'? quia uera quidem, sed non ex semine: de statu similis et uera, de censu non uero dissimilis. ceterum similitudo in contrariis nulla est. spiritus non diceretur carnis similitudo, — quia nec caro similitudinem spiritus caperet — sed phantasma diceretur, si id quod non erat uidebatur. similitudo autem dicitur, cum est quod uidetur. est enim, dum alterius par est. phantasma autem, qua hoc tantum est, non est similitudo. Et hic autem ipse edisserens, quomodo nolit nos esse in carne, cum simus in carne, ut scilicet non simus in operibus carnis, ostendit hac ratione scripsisse: caro et sanguis regnum dei non consequentur, non substantiam damnans, sed opera eius; quae, (quia) possunt non admitti a nobis in carne adhuc positis, non ad reatum substantiae, sed ad conuersationispertinebunt. Item si corpusquidem mortuum propter delictum, — adeo non animae, sed corporis mors est - spiritus autem uita propter iustitiam, *** cui mors obuenit propter delictum, id est corpori. non enim alii quid restituitur, nisi qui illud amisit, et ita erit resurrectio. mortuorum dum est, corporum. nam et subiungit: qui suscitauit Christum a mortuis, uiuificabit et mortalia corpora uestra. adeo et carnis resurrectionem confirmauit, absque qua nec corpus aliquid dici capit nec mortale aliquid intellegi, et Christi substantiam corporalem probauit; siquidem proinde uiuificabuntur et mortalia corpora nostra, quemadmodum et ille resuscitatus est, non alias proinde, nisi quia in corpore.
pass_a_gloss: If the Father sent Him in the likeness of sinful flesh, therefore the flesh which was seen in Him will not be called a phantom because of this. For He assigned sin to the flesh and made it a law of sin dwelling in its members and opposing the law of the mind. Therefore, the Son was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that He might redeem the flesh of sin with a similar substance, that is, with flesh which would be similar to sinful flesh, although it would not be sinful itself. For this will be the power of God in a similar substance to bring about salvation. For it is not a great thing if the Spirit of God were to heal the flesh, but if the flesh, similar to sinful flesh, while being flesh, but not sin, does so. Thus, the likeness will pertain to the title of sin, not to a lie about the substance. For if He had wanted the likeness of the substance to be understood, so that He might deny the truth, He would have only said 'flesh', not 'flesh of sin'. But when He constructed it in this way: 'flesh of sin', He confirmed the substance, that is, the flesh, and referred the likeness to the vice of the substance, that is, to sin. Suppose now the likeness of the substance is spoken of: the truth of the substance will not be denied because of this. (Why, then, is it similar, if it is true? Because it is true, indeed, but not from the seed; similar and true in terms of state, but not similar in terms of origin.) Moreover, there is no likeness in opposites. The Spirit would not be called the likeness of flesh - (for flesh would not take on the likeness of Spirit) - but would be called a phantom, if that which is not were seen. But likeness is spoken of when there is something that is seen, for it is, while being equal to another. A phantom, however, which is only this, is not a likeness. And He Himself, explaining in this way that He does not want us to be in the flesh, since we are in the flesh, so that we may not be in the works of the flesh, shows that He wrote (1 Corinthians 15:50) 'Flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God' not condemning the substance, but its works; which, because they can be rejected by us while we are still in the flesh, pertain not to the guilt of the substance, but to our conduct. Likewise, if the body is dead because of sin - so much so that death is of the body, not of the soul - but the Spirit is life because of righteousness, to which death comes because of sin, that is, to the body, for nothing is restored except to him who lost it, and thus there will be a resurrection of the dead, while it is of bodies. For He also adds: 'He who raised Christ from the dead will give life to your mortal bodies.' Thus, He confirmed the resurrection of the flesh, without which neither can a body be called anything, nor can anything mortal be understood, and He proved the bodily substance of Christ; for just as He was raised, so our mortal bodies will be given life, not otherwise, but because they are in a body.

bible_refs.note: Flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God

pass_b_english: When the Father sent the Son in a body that resembled sinful human flesh, that didn't make the Son's body an illusion. The reason is that sin had become a kind of law, dwelling in the body and opposing the mind's intentions. So, the Son was sent to redeem our sinful bodies, and He did this by taking on a body similar to ours, yet without sin. This is how God's power works: by using a similar substance to bring about salvation. It's not particularly impressive if the Holy Spirit can heal the body, but it's a different story when the body itself, similar to our sinful bodies yet without sin, is the agent of healing. In this way, the likeness is related to sin, not to any deception about the nature of the body. If the goal was to deny the truth about the body, the phrase would have been simply 'flesh', not 'flesh of sin'. But by saying 'flesh of sin', the substance - the body - is confirmed, and the likeness is related to the sin that affects the body. Suppose we're talking about the likeness of the body itself: that doesn't mean the body's true nature is being denied. The question is, why would something true be called similar? The answer is that it's similar in terms of its state, but not its origin - it's true, but not from the same source. Moreover, things that are opposites can't be similar. The Spirit can't be said to resemble the body, and if something that isn't real appears to be real, it's an illusion, not a likeness. A likeness implies something that actually exists and is comparable to something else. An illusion, on the other hand, is just that - an appearance without reality. The Lord Himself explains that He doesn't want us to be controlled by our bodies, even though we're in them, so that we won't be controlled by our bodily desires. As He writes in 1 Corinthians 15:50, 'Flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God' - He's not condemning the body itself, but its actions, which we can reject even while we're still in our bodies. This isn't about the body being guilty, but about how we conduct ourselves. Similarly, when the body dies because of sin, that's a death of the body, not the soul. But the Spirit is life, and death comes to the body because of sin. The point is that only what has been lost can be restored, and that's why there will be a resurrection of the dead - a resurrection of bodies. As the Lord also says, 'He who raised Christ from the dead will give life to your mortal bodies.' This confirms that the body will be resurrected, which is necessary if we're to understand what a body is and what it means to be mortal. It also proves that Christ had a real body, and just as He was raised from the dead, our mortal bodies will be given life, because they are bodies, just like His.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions regarding substance versus vice/sin. Pass A is a faithful translation of the Latin. Pass B is a fluent rendering that preserves the meaning and nuances of the original, including the distinction between 'state' and 'origin' (de statu similis et uera, de censu non uero dissimilis) and the distinction between substance and works. Scripture citations (1 Corinthians 15:50) are correctly identified and applied to the relevant text.

source: 'Hunc si pater misit in similitudinem carnis peccati, non ideo phantasma dicetur caro, quae in illo uidebatur.', English: 'When the Father sent the Son in a body that resembled sinful human flesh, that didn't make the Son's body an illusion.'
